analysis.one_liner: Requires private equity and for-profit owners of hospitals and clinics to disclose finances and get federal approval to invest.
analysis.headline: The Health Over Wealth Act, introduced July 23, 2026 by Rep. Jayapal with two Democratic cosponsors, sits with four House committees; no hearing or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets private equity and other for-profit owners of hospitals, doctor practices, nursing homes, and hospices. It would force them to report their debts, fees, staffing levels, closures, and political spending to the Health Department, make that data public, and require private equity firms to get a federal license — which can be revoked — before investing in health care. It also lets the Secretary put a hold on private equity takeovers of health care firms, restricts sale-leaseback deals with real estate trusts, adds a new tax rule aimed at health care real estate trusts, and requires hospitals to give 90 days' notice before closing or cutting essential services, with public comment and a mitigation plan. It even orders research on the impact of an outright ban on for-profit ownership of health care.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in communities served by private equity- or for-profit-owned hospitals and clinics, health care workers facing understaffing and wage cuts, and communities at risk of losing a hospital. The bill also steers licensing fees to the National Health Service Corps, community health centers, teaching health centers, and hospitals serving low-income patients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, health workers, and underserved communities

how_it_helps.text: Requires for-profit health care owners, especially private equity-backed ones, to publicly report debt loads, fees charged to hospitals, dividends extracted, staffing ratios, staff retention, facility closures, wage cuts, and labor law complaints [S2].

Requires private equity firms to obtain a federal license to invest in health care, which the Secretary can deny or revoke for price gouging, understaffing, or access barriers — and a revoked firm must divest [S2].

Lets the Secretary require private equity-controlled firms to set aside five years of operating funds in escrow, and allows a moratorium on private equity takeovers of health care firms while a new task force studies abuses [S2].

Requires hospitals to notify the Secretary at least 90 days before closing or dropping essential services, keeps those services running during the notice period, and opens the decision to public comment, with possible Medicare enrollment bans for violators [S2].
Routes licensing and penalty fees to the National Health Service Corps, community health centers, teaching health centers, and hospitals serving disproportionate numbers of low-income patients [S2].

In bankruptcy, puts health care workers' pension withdrawal liability first in line ahead of other creditors, and requires courts weighing a hospital's bankruptcy plan to give substantial weight to regional access to care [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, for-profit hospital and nursing home operators, and health care real estate investment trusts, which face new disclosure costs, licensing, escrow requirements, restrictions on sale-leaseback deals, and a tax change that would strip favorable treatment from rents on health care property. Compliance costs could be passed through to patients or discourage investment in struggling facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity, for-profit operators, health care REITs

drawbacks.text: The disclosure regime is sweeping — up to 38 categories of information covering 10 years of history — and even though the bill directs the Secretary to reduce duplication and administrative burden, compliance costs for hospitals and nursing home operators could be significant and could be passed to patients [S2].

Licensing and a possible moratorium on private equity acquisitions concentrate sweeping discretionary power in the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and could discourage investment in rural and financially struggling hospitals that may lack other buyers [S2].
The tax change for health care property rents applies to taxable years after enactment, immediately raising costs for real estate trusts that own hospital buildings without a transition period [S2].
The $10,000-per-violation civil penalty in the general enforcement section is small relative to health system revenues, potentially limiting the deterrence of the reporting requirements [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities where private equity-owned hospitals or nursing homes have cut staff, closed, or been loaded with debt, the transparency, licensing, and closure-notice provisions address documented, serious harms. The trade-offs are real: heavy compliance burdens, broad discretionary power in one cabinet secretary, and a risk that new friction discourages capital from facilities that need it. The bill is more of a framework and study bill — including research on a full ban on for-profit ownership — than a finished regulatory design, and its main immediate effect would be sunlight on ownership and finances.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 23, 2026 and sent to four House committees — Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — and none of them has taken it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on July 23, 2026, joined by Reps. Chris Deluzio and Yvette Clarke [S2].
The bill was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, Ways and Means, and the Judiciary for consideration of the provisions within each committee's jurisdiction [S4].
The bill has two cosponsors listed, both Democrats [S3].
No hearings, markups, or floor votes appear in the action history since introduction [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill parked across four committees and no movement, private equity funds, for-profit health care operators, and health care real estate trusts continue operating under current rules — including existing tax advantages for health care real estate trusts and no federal licensing to buy hospitals or nursing homes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and for-profit health care investors, so far

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors are Democrats; no Republican cosponsors are listed, and with the bill pending in committee no votes have occurred to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill requires private equity funds controlling health care firms to disclose fees, debt loads, dividends extracted, staffing cuts, and political spending; to buy a federal license to invest; to post five years of operating reserves; and it allows a moratorium on their takeovers. The fundable model — buying hospitals and nursing homes, loading them with debt, and collecting management fees — is what the disclosure and licensing regime targets, and patients and workers are the people those practices have cost.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill bars hospitals from sale-leaseback deals with REITs whose terms would weaken the hospital's finances or public health, and rewrites the tax code so rents from health care property no longer qualify for REIT treatment, ending a favorable tax status. Communities with closed or financially drained hospitals bear the other side of those sale-leaseback arrangements.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital and nursing home operators
industries.note: For-profit firms that own health care entities face sweeping disclosure requirements — staffing ratios, closures, wage cuts, executive pay — plus escrow and closure-notice rules with possible Medicare enrollment bans. Some operators deliver needed care in their markets, but the bill is built around evidence that ownership structures have been linked to understaffing, closures, and reduced access.

A new Investment Company Act provision makes it unlawful for registered investment companies to strip assets from health care entities or undermine care quality or access, with SEC rules to define prohibited conduct. Most funds would be unaffected, but asset-stripping structures involving health care holdings would be blocked.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety-net providers
industries.note: Licensing application fees and civil penalties are dedicated to the National Health Service Corps, community health centers, teaching health centers, and hospitals serving low-income patients, providing a new funding stream for care in underserved areas.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to four committees with three sponsors and no bipartisan cosponsors almost never reach the House floor on their own; the split referral to Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary makes a markup especially unlikely. The realistic paths are stalling in committee until the Congress ends, or individual provisions — such as hospital closure notification or private equity disclosure — being folded into a larger health care or spending package.
